name: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics
description: Two adjacent, non-identical Greek frameworks gathered under one school because both use the word pathē (πάθη, roughly "that which is undergone") and both come out of the same fourth-to-third-century BCE philosophical culture in Athens — not because they agree with each other. Aristotle's Rhetoric (Book II) catalogues pathē as states a speaker can arouse in an audience to make a case land: they are appraisals bound to a rhetorical situation (who feels this, toward whom, and on what belief), not a clinical inventory of inner states. The Stoics, from Zeno and Chrysippus onward, use pathē in a stricter and more critical sense — an irrational, excessive impulse that follows from a false judgment about what is good or bad, which the wise person replaces with a calibrated "good feeling" (eupatheia) rather than simply having less of. Treating Aristotle's rhetorical pathē and Stoic ethical pathē as one undifferentiated "Greek emotion theory" flattens a real disagreement between them about what pathē even are.

_note: Skeleton, not a finished catalogue. Aristotle names fourteen pathē across Rhetoric II.1–11 (anger/calm, love/hatred, fear/confidence, shame/shamelessness, kindness, pity/indignation, envy/emulation, contempt); only anger (orgē) and pity (eleos) are written here as representative items. The Stoics' four canonical pathē (lypē, phobos, epithymia, hēdonē) are all present, but the many named species later Stoic doxographers catalogue under each genus are not. No cross-links to other schools in this collection have been added yet.

_art_direction.period_place: Athens and the wider Greek world, 5th–3rd century BCE — Attic red-figure and black-figure vase painting fits Aristotle's audience-facing, gesture-based pathe best. No comparably rich visual record survives specifically for the early Stoa, so the same vase-painting culture (Zeno taught in Athens a generation after Aristotle, in the Stoa Poikile the school is named for) is the nearest honest fit for both halves of this school.

attribution.name: Aristotle
attribution.note: Structural basis for the rhetorical half of this school: Rhetoric, Book II (4th century BCE), on the pathē an orator can arouse in an audience. The Rhetoric is long out of copyright; no modern translator's specific wording is quoted — every section here is original prose describing Aristotle's categories, not a translation excerpt.

attribution.name: Zeno of Citium and the early Stoa
attribution.note: Structural basis for the Stoic half: the four-genus classification of pathē (distress, fear, desire, pleasure) and the three eupatheiai, known to us mainly through later doxography (Diogenes Laërtius, Stobaeus). No modern translator's wording is quoted; descriptions are original prose.

sections.Definition: In Rhetoric II.2, Aristotle defines anger (orgē) as a desire, accompanied by pain, for conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous and unjustified slight directed at oneself or someone close to one. It is not raw physiological arousal; it is an appraisal — a judgment that one has been wronged and belittled — paired with the expectation that retaliation will be pleasant.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle is not describing anger as a state to be diagnosed or managed. He is telling an orator which beliefs make an audience angry — being slighted by people who owe them respect — so a speech can provoke that anger against an opponent, or calm it (praotēs, the paired state) in a judge who has been roused against the speaker's own client.
sections.Research note: Aristotle treats anger as an object-directed judgment rather than a mood — a cognitive-appraisal reading of emotion that anticipates, without duplicating, both Stoic theory and modern appraisal theories such as Richard Lazarus's (1991).

metadata.image_credit: Terracotta volute-krater with battle scene (Amazonomachy), Greek, Attic, ca. 450 BCE — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain / CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.8 defines pity (eleos) as pain at an apparently destructive or painful event happening to someone who does not deserve it, which the observer might expect could happen to himself or someone close to him. Both conditions matter: the suffering must look undeserved, and the observer must see it as possible for themselves — Aristotle notes that people who feel invulnerable feel less pity.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Pity here is a lever, not a syndrome. Aristotle catalogues what makes a courtroom audience pity a defendant — visible, specific, nearby suffering, a person like the listener — because a speaker who understands the lever can pull it.
sections.Research note: Aristotle explicitly pairs eleos with nemesis (indignation at another's undeserved good fortune) as mirror-image judgments about desert, not as unrelated feelings — a structural pairing this skeleton does not yet include as its own item.

sections.Definition: In the Stoic scheme reported by later sources (chiefly Diogenes Laërtius and Stobaeus), lypē is an irrational contraction of the soul at what is wrongly judged to be a present evil. It is one of the four canonical pathē — a mistaken value-judgment about the present, not a physiological given.
sections.Why the Stoics call it irrational: For the Stoics, only virtue and vice are genuinely good or bad; everything else — health, wealth, reputation, even bodily pain — is "indifferent." Lypē arises from judging one of those indifferents to be a real evil. Because the judgment is false, the Stoics hold there is no well-reasoned version of it — unlike the other three pathē, lypē has no eupatheia (rational good-feeling) counterpart in the sage.
sections.Research note: This is an ethical claim about which judgments are true, not a description of a bodily process — reading lypē as equivalent to the modern clinical category "depression," or flattening it to the modern English word "distress," overstates the overlap in both directions.

metadata.image_credit: Terracotta lekythos (oil flask), tomb scene, Greek, Attic, ca. 440 BCE — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain / CC0 (Open Access). White-ground lekythoi of this type were funerary offerings, commonly painted with mourning-at-the-tomb scenes.

sections.Definition: Phobos, in the Stoic scheme, is an irrational shrinking-away from an expected evil — the future-facing counterpart to lypē's present-facing contraction. Like the other three pathē it is a judgment: that some coming indifferent is a real evil worth fleeing.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Fear's eupatheia is eulabeia, usually translated "caution" — a well-reasoned aversion to a genuine evil (vice, a wrong action) rather than to an indifferent thing. A Stoic sage, on this account, still avoids stepping off a cliff; the claim concerns which judgment does the avoiding, not the removal of self-preservation.
sections.Research note: The eupatheiai are attributed only to the sage — an ideal the Stoics themselves treat as rarely, if ever, instantiated. This is a normative model of how judgment should work, not a description of how most people's fear does work.

metadata.image_credit: Terracotta lekythos (oil flask) depicting Perseus, Medusa, and Pegasus, Greek, Attic, ca. 500 BCE — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain / CC0 (Open Access). The Gorgon's head is the standard Greek apotropaic image of terror.

sections.Definition: Epithymia is an irrational reaching-toward a future indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the desire-pole of the Stoic four, paired conceptually with hēdonē (pleasure) the way phobos is paired with lypē: future versus present, in each case built on a mistaken value-judgment.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Epithymia's eupatheia is boulēsis, "wish" or rational will — desire aimed only at what is genuinely worth wanting: wisdom, justice, courage, self-command. The Stoics did not hold that a sage desires nothing; they held that a sage desires correctly.
sections.Research note: Later Stoic sources subdivide epithymia into a long list of named species — anger itself is sometimes classed as a form of it, a desire for revenge. This item covers the genus, not its species.

metadata.image_credit: Terracotta statuette of Eros, Greek, probably Attic, first half of the 4th century BCE — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain / CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Hēdonē is an irrational swelling of the soul at a present indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the present-facing counterpart to epithymia's future reach, and structurally opposite to lypē.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Hēdonē's eupatheia is chara, "joy" — a well-founded elation at something genuinely good, namely virtuous action itself, rather than at an indifferent circumstance. The Stoics distinguish chara sharply from hēdonē: the same felt shape, resting on a different object and a different judgment.
sections.Research note: Later Stoics, especially the Roman Stoic Seneca, develop chara at length as a durable good feeling available regardless of external circumstance — an idea with obvious later influence on Christian and secular therapeutic traditions, none of which this item claims as Stoic in origin.

metadata.image_credit: Terracotta kylix (drinking cup), men drinking (symposium scene), Greek, Attic, ca. 480-470 BCE — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain / CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Two of the fourteen pathē Aristotle catalogues in Rhetoric Book II as levers an orator can pull in an audience — states defined by who feels them, toward whom, and under what belief, not by an inner sensation alone.

The Stoics' complete top-level classification: two temporal axes (present, future) crossed with two valences (wrongly judged good, wrongly judged bad), all four built on a false value-judgment, and all but lypē paired with a "good feeling" (eupatheia) available to the wise.

items.name: Greek Pathē — the Rhetorical and Stoic Readings

sections.Definition: Two Greek philosophical traditions used the same word, pathē, for genuinely different projects. Aristotle's Rhetoric treats pathē as persuasion-relevant judgments an audience can be moved into or out of — the concern is rhetorical effectiveness, not moral evaluation of the feeling itself. The Stoa treats pathē as a technical term for a specific kind of error: an irrational, excessive impulse built on a false judgment about what is good or bad, which the wise person replaces with a calibrated "good feeling" rather than simply feeling it less.
sections.Research note: Neither tradition offers an empirical account of emotion in the modern sense — no physiology, no cross-cultural measurement. Both are philosophical: one about persuasion, one about ethics and right judgment. Later cognitive-appraisal theories of emotion (Richard Lazarus; Robert Solomon; Martha Nussbaum's explicitly neo-Stoic Upheavals of Thought, 2001) draw structural inspiration from the idea that an emotion involves a judgment, without claiming empirical continuity with either ancient text.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial — Recursive Repatterning's own commentary, not a claim either tradition made.* Both frameworks already treat pathē as judgment-dependent and context-bound rather than as a fixed inner essence — closer, in that one respect, to a constructed-emotion reading than many later "basic emotion" accounts are. Where they part ways with a constructionist account is in assuming there is a single correct judgment (Stoic) or a stable, reliably-producible target state (Aristotle) — the constructionist alternative holds that even the categories used to name the judgment are themselves learned and variable, not universal.

metadata.evidence_note: Both frameworks are philosophical argument, not empirical research — the Rhetoric is a handbook for persuasion and the Stoic pathē scheme is an ethical claim about which judgments are true. Neither offers, or claims to offer, cross-cultural or physiological evidence; assessing them by that standard would be a category error the traditions themselves did not intend.
